351.title: Seeing it is seeing
351.hook: whoever sees dependent origination sees the dhamma (MN 28)
351.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often pair the line from MN 28 with the Buddha's words to Vakkali to explain that the teaching, not the teacher's body, is what students are meant to see.

segments.voice: Yesterday: where the chain breaks, and your line, cut between. Did you feel a first arrow, and skip the second, even once? Day three hundred fifty-one.

A monk named Vakkali lies gravely ill in a potter's shed. Tradition says he had loved the Buddha so much that he followed him around just to look at his face. Now the Buddha comes to his bedside, and Vakkali stirs, trying to get up. For a long time, he says, he'd wanted to come and see the Blessed One, but his body hadn't let him. The Buddha's answer turns what seeing means inside out. Today, we come back to the elephant's footprint, where this block began.
screen: `VAKKALI, GRAVELY ILL.` → `A BEDSIDE VISIT.` → `WHAT SEEING MEANS.`

segments.voice: Here's what the Buddha told Vakkali, in the Connected Discourses. Enough, Vakkali. Why do you want to see this rotting body? Whoever sees the Dhamma sees me; whoever sees me sees the Dhamma. It isn't cold. It's a gift: you don't need my face; you need what I've been pointing at. Now go back to the very first day of this block, the elephant's footprint, Sariputta's great talk in the Middle-Length Discourses. Near its end, after walking through the body's elements and the five heaps, Sariputta quotes the Buddha with a line that has the same shape. Whoever sees dependent origination sees the Dhamma. Whoever sees the Dhamma sees dependent origination. Put the two together and something comes into focus. To see the Buddha is to see the Dhamma. To see the Dhamma is to see dependent arising: this, because of that. So in these two suttas, the seeing that counts isn't of a person or a place or a vision. It's seeing how things lean on each other. How a mood leans on sleep. How craving leans on feeling. How dukkha leans on craving, and ends when craving ends. Sariputta draws the conclusion right there in the sutta: the five heaps are dependently arisen, and the desire and clinging for them is the origin of dukkha. Seeing it isn't a step before the real thing. The seeing is the real thing. That's why the title repeats itself: seeing it is seeing.
screen: `WHOEVER SEES THE DHAMMA SEES ME.` · `BACK TO THE ELEPHANT'S FOOTPRINT.` · `TO SEE DEPENDENT ARISING.` · `THE SEEING IS THE REAL THING.` · then, large: `SEEING IT IS SEEING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to see one connection clearly. Sit and breathe. Choose one small thing happening in you right now: a sound you hear, an ache, a thought. Ask what it depends on. The sound depends on the ear, the air, the source. The ache depends on how you're sitting. Stay with just one link until you can see it plainly, without commentary. Then rest, and let the seeing be enough. The bell holds the time.
Seeing it is seeing. Whoever sees dependent arising sees the Dhamma, and whoever sees the Dhamma sees the Buddha.
Your line: seeing it is seeing. Today, when you understand why something happened, pause and notice that the understanding itself is a kind of seeing. Day three hundred fifty-one.

match.prompt: match each line to who said or heard it.
pairs: wanted to see the Buddha's body

myth: the Buddha told Vakkali to keep gazing at him
he said: why see this body? whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
MN 28, the elephant's footprint, contains the line about dependent origination
Sariputta quotes it near the end of the talk.
in MN 28, seeing the Dhamma means having a vision of light
it means seeing dependent arising: how things lean on each other.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha, at the bedside of a sick monk who has always longed to look at you. he tries to get up to see you. what do you say?
options: stay and look at me as long as you like.
why see this body? whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.
you must get well before you see me.
fork.reveal: the Buddha turned Vakkali's eyes from his body to the teaching: whoever sees the Dhamma sees me.

original.note: Pali dhamma, Sanskrit dharma: the teaching, and the way things are, which the teaching points to.

trapdoor: what you thought: seeing the Dhamma is a mystical vision.
what it means: it's seeing how things arise from conditions, and how dukkha ends when its conditions end.
what a scholar hears: MN 28 has Sariputta cite yo paṭiccasamuppādaṃ passati so dhammaṃ passati, and SN 22.87 has yo kho dhammaṃ passati so maṃ passati; both make seeing the teaching the true meeting.

sources.ref: MN 28 (Mahahatthipadopama Sutta), the line on dependent origination

352.title: The truths, closed
352.hook: four truths, three turns, twelve links
352.howItsDone: Buddhist schools teach the four noble truths as a core of the Dhamma; in Theravada communities the first sermon, which sets them out, is often chanted in Pali, notably on the full moon of Asalha.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seeing it is seeing, and your line, seeing it is seeing. Did understanding why something happened feel like a kind of seeing? Today, we close the four truths. Day three hundred fifty-two.

At the end of a long hike, some people turn around at the trailhead and look back up at the mountain. From down here it looks small, a single shape against the sky. But the hiker remembers every switchback: where the path got steep, where they sat on a rock, where the view opened. Three weeks ago, year two began at an elephant's footprint, with Sariputta saying that every wholesome thing fits inside four truths. Today we stand at the bottom and look back up at those four, before the path turns toward the eight.
screen: `LOOKING BACK UP THE MOUNTAIN.` → `EVERY SWITCHBACK.` → `FOUR TRUTHS, BEFORE THE EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole block. It began with the elephant's footprint, the print that holds all others, and a physician's pattern: illness, cause, cure, treatment. Then the first truth in full: birth, aging, sickness, death, not getting what you want. Three kinds of dukkha: pain, change, and the unease of made things. Its task: to be understood. The second truth, samudaya, three thirsts, and its task: to be let go, like a wish that ends at the park. The third, nirodha: it can stop, the burden set down. Nibbana, the fire gone out. Its task: to be realized, tasted like the ocean's salt. The fourth, magga, the eightfold path, and its task: to be developed, walked into being. Three turns and twelve aspects: the Buddha's own checklist before he claimed awakening. A handful of leaves: only what helps. The poisoned arrow: treat the wound first. The blind turtle: a rare life, so look into the truths. And underneath it all, paticcasamuppada, this because of that, laid out in twelve links, with a seam between feeling and craving where the chain can break. And seeing that is seeing the Dhamma. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, gathers the four truths into a single line: "pain, the origin of pain, the destruction of pain, and the eightfold holy way that leads to the quieting of pain." One way to read the list: three of the four truths are set up for the last one. Understand, let go, realize: all of it gets done by walking. That's where we go next. Block B takes the eightfold path one factor at a time, starting tomorrow with how the eight fit together.
screen: `FOOTPRINT, PHYSICIAN, FIRST TRUTH.` · `FOUR TRUTHS, FOUR TASKS.` · `LEAVES, ARROW, TURTLE.` · `THIS BECAUSE OF THAT, IN TWELVE LINKS.` · then, large: `FOUR TRUTHS, ONE PATH.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sit with all four. Settle, and let the breath find its rhythm. On the first breath, think: dukkha, to be understood. On the second: craving, to be let go. On the third: its ending, to be realized. On the fourth: the path, to be developed. Then let the words fall away, and just sit inside the shape they make, like resting at the trailhead. If the mind wanders, begin again at the first. The bell holds the time.
The truths. The four noble truths, each with its task, known in three turns, and resting on dependent arising: the elephant's footprint, walked all the way around.
Your line: four truths, one path. Today, say the four truths once, out loud or under your breath, and notice that the fourth one is something you can do today. Day three hundred fifty-two.

match.prompt: match each piece of the block to what it taught.
pairs: all wholesome things fit in four truths
treat the wound before asking who
this is, to be done, done

myth: each of the four truths has the same task
understand, let go, realize, develop: one verb each.
the Dhammapada sums up the four truths in one line
in Müller's version: pain, its origin, its destruction, and the eightfold holy way.
dependent arising has nothing to do with the four truths
it shows how dukkha arises from conditions and how it can end.

fork.setup: you've walked all four truths. understand, let go, realize, develop. which one of these is done by walking?
options: only the first.
the fourth, and through it, the other three.
none: they're only ideas.
fork.reveal: the path is the one truth to be developed, and walking it is how dukkha gets understood, craving let go, and the ending realized.

original.note: Pali ariyasacca: noble truth; the four ariyasaccāni are the heart of the first sermon.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four truths are a list to agree with.
what it means: four truths with four tasks, all walked through one path.
what a scholar hears: ariyasacca can be read as truth of the noble ones or noble truth; the Saccasaṃyutta (SN 56) gathers a whole collection of short suttas around these four.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)

353.title: Eight spokes, one wheel
353.hook: the eight factors in three trainings: wisdom, conduct, meditation (MN 44)
353.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers commonly teach the eightfold path through the three trainings of conduct, meditation and wisdom, and the eight-spoked dharma wheel appears on temples, flags and books across Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the truths, closed, and your line, four truths, one path. Did you say the four once, and notice the fourth is something to do? Today the path itself opens. Day three hundred fifty-three.

The commentaries tell the backstory. A merchant named Visakha comes home from hearing the Buddha teach, changed for good, and his wife, Dhammadinna, notices. Soon she goes forth as a nun, practices hard, and, tradition says, becomes fully awakened. One day Visakha visits her, and instead of small talk, he asks her question after question about the teaching. She answers every one. When he reports the conversation to the Buddha, the Buddha says he would have answered exactly the same way. One of Visakha's questions is about how the eightfold path fits together. Today, a block begins: the path, factor by factor.
screen: `VISAKHA'S WIFE BECOMES A NUN.` → `QUESTION AFTER QUESTION.` → `I'D HAVE ANSWERED THE SAME.`

segments.voice: The conversation is in the Middle-Length Discourses, number forty-four. Visakha asks: are the three trainings included in the noble eightfold path, or is the path included in the three trainings? Dhammadinna answers that the eight are sorted into the three. Right speech, right action and right livelihood belong to conduct, sila: how you live with others. Right effort, right mindfulness and right concentration belong to meditation, samadhi: how you train the mind. Right view and right intention belong to wisdom, panna: how you see, and what you aim for. Eight factors, three trainings. Now the wheel. The dharma wheel with eight spokes is a later symbol, carved and painted all over Asia; you'll find it on temple gates and flags. But it fits Dhammadinna's answer. A wheel with a missing spoke still turns, badly. A wheel with all eight runs true. And no spoke comes first: they all meet at the hub and all touch the rim at once. The path's own list starts with right view, so some teachers say wisdom comes first: you need a view to start walking. Dhammadinna names conduct first, so others say a calm, honest life is the ground for everything else. Both orders are in the texts. What they agree on is that the three trainings lean on each other, like the spokes. Over the next weeks, we'll take each spoke on its own, starting tomorrow with right view. And it's worth remembering who drew this map: a nun, whose answers the Buddha said he would have given himself.
screen: `DHAMMADINNA SORTS THE EIGHT.` · `CONDUCT, MEDITATION, WISDOM.` · `A WHEEL WITH EIGHT SPOKES.` · `THE TRAININGS LEAN ON EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `EIGHT SPOKES, ONE WHEEL.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to sort the eight into three. Sit, and picture three bowls in front of you: conduct, meditation, wisdom. Breathe, and drop each factor into its bowl. Speech, action, livelihood: into conduct. Effort, mindfulness, concentration: into meditation. View, intention: into wisdom. Then picture the three bowls set around a single wheel, and let the wheel turn slowly with your breath. The bell holds the time.
Eight spokes. The eight factors of the path, sorted by the nun Dhammadinna into three trainings: conduct, meditation and wisdom, all turning together.

Your line: eight spokes, one wheel. Today, notice one moment where one training leans on another: how a calmer mind changes your speech, or how honest speech settles the mind. Day three hundred fifty-three.

match.prompt: match each factor to its training.
pairs: the nun who sorted the eight

myth: the eight-spoked wheel appears in the first sermon
it's a later symbol; the sermon speaks of setting the wheel rolling but doesn't count spokes.
the Buddha said he would have answered Visakha just as Dhammadinna did
he approved her answers in MN 44.
right effort belongs to the training in wisdom
Dhammadinna puts effort, mindfulness and concentration under meditation.

fork.setup: you're Visakha. you've just heard Dhammadinna's answers and reported them to the Buddha. what does he say?
options: she got some of it wrong.
he would have answered the same way.
a nun shouldn't teach a layman.
fork.reveal: the Buddha says Dhammadinna is wise, and that he would have explained it exactly as she did.

original.note: Pali sikkhā: training; the three trainings are conduct (sīla), meditation (samādhi) and wisdom (paññā).

trapdoor: what you thought: the eightfold path is eight separate rules.
what it means: eight factors that sort into three trainings, all working together like spokes.

what a scholar hears: in MN 44 Dhammadinnā says the three khandhas (sīla, samādhi, paññā) include the path, not the path the three; the eight-spoked wheel as an emblem is attested later in Buddhist art.

354.title: Right view
354.hook: knowing dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way (MN 9)
354.howItsDone: The Sammaditthi Sutta, Sariputta's talk on right view, is studied in Theravada monasteries, and teachers in several schools describe right view as seeing through the lens of the four truths.

segments.voice: Yesterday: eight spokes, and your line, eight spokes, one wheel. Did you catch one training leaning on another? Today, the first spoke. Day three hundred fifty-four.

Put on someone else's glasses and the world tilts. The edges blur, the floor seems closer, you reach for a cup and miss. Nothing in the room changed. Only the lens did. Right view, the first factor of the eightfold path, is about the lens. And a long explanation of it comes not from the Buddha but from Sariputta again, in a talk where the monks keep asking, politely, for more. Each time, he finds another way to say it. Today, right view.
screen: `SOMEONE ELSE'S GLASSES.` → `ONLY THE LENS CHANGED.` → `THE MONKS KEEP ASKING.`

segments.voice: The Pali is samma ditthi. Ditthi means view: a way of seeing. Samma, as we've heard, means right, complete, fitting. The talk is the ninth in the Middle-Length Discourses. Sariputta asks the monks: in what way is a disciple of right view, whose view is straight? They ask him to explain. And he does it in a pattern he repeats again and again. When someone understands the unwholesome and its root, the wholesome and its root, that is right view. The monks say, good, friend, and then ask: but might there be another way? Yes, he says, and he explains it through food and nourishment. Then again through the four truths: understanding dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way to its ending. Then again through each of the twelve links: aging and death, its arising, its ending, the way. Around and around, with the same four-part shape. So right view here isn't mainly a set of opinions to sign. It's a way of looking at anything: what is this, where does it come from, can it end, and how? Another sutta in the Connected Discourses, defining all eight factors, gives the short form: right view is knowledge of dukkha, its arising, its ending, and the way. That's the lens. Notice that the four truths aren't only a teaching to remember. They're also glasses to see through. A bad night's sleep, a fight with a sibling, a fear about money: each can be looked at the same four ways. For Sariputta, that's what makes a view right: it looks at anything in terms of where it comes from and how it ends.
screen: `DITTHI: VIEW, A WAY OF SEEING.` · `MIGHT THERE BE ANOTHER WAY?` · `THE SAME FOUR-PART SHAPE.` · `THE TRUTHS AS GLASSES.` · then, large: `SEE IT AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to look at one event with that lens. Sit, and bring to mind one small thing that happened recently that bothered you. Look at it four ways, slowly, a few breaths each. What is it, plainly? Where did it come from? Could it ease or end? What would help? You don't need answers that are perfect. Just try on the glasses, and notice whether the event looks different through them. The bell holds the time.
Samma ditthi. Right view: knowing dukkha, its arising, its ending and the way, the four truths used as a lens. The first factor of the path.
Your line: see it as it is. Today, when something goes sideways, ask the four questions: what is it, where's it from, can it end, what helps. Day three hundred fifty-four.

match.prompt: match the pieces of right view.
pairs: knowing dukkha, its arising, ending, way

myth: in MN 9 Sariputta gives only one explanation of right view
the monks keep asking for another way, and he gives many, all with the same shape.
right view can be defined as knowing the four truths
that's the short form given in the sutta that defines the eight factors.
right view here mainly means signing up to a set of opinions
it's a way of seeing anything: what it is, its source, its ending, and the way.

fork.setup: you're one of the monks. Sariputta has just explained right view through wholesome and unwholesome roots. what do you ask?
options: that's enough, thank you.
but might there be another way to explain it?
which teacher is right about this?
fork.reveal: the monks keep asking for another way, and Sariputta keeps finding one: food, the four truths, each of the twelve links.

original.note: Pali sammā diṭṭhi: right view, the first factor of the eightfold path.

trapdoor: what you thought: right view means having the correct beliefs.
what it means: seeing anything through the four truths: what it is, where it comes from, its ending, the way.

what a scholar hears: MN 9 gives some sixteen explanations, most in the four-part pattern, running through each of the twelve links, and SN 45.8 defines sammā diṭṭhi as dukkhe ñāṇa, knowledge of dukkha, its arising, ending and way.

sources.ref: MN 9 (Sammaditthi Sutta, Sariputta on right view)

355.title: Roots
355.hook: Sariputta: the roots of the unwholesome are greed, hate and delusion; their opposites are the wholesome roots (MN 9)
355.howItsDone: Buddhist teaching across schools names the three unwholesome roots, greed, hatred and delusion, and the ten courses of action; some practitioners reflect at the end of the day on which roots their actions came from.

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma ditthi, right view, and your line, see it as it is. Did you try the four questions on something that went sideways? Day three hundred fifty-five.
screen: `SAMMA DITTHI — SEE IT AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Anyone who's pulled weeds knows the trick. Snap off the top and you've done nothing; next week it's back, greener than before. You have to get your fingers down into the soil and ease out the root, the pale stringy part you never see. The first answer Sariputta gives in his talk on right view is about exactly this. Before the four truths, before the twelve links, he starts with actions and the roots they grow from. Today, the word for what grows from good roots: kusala.
screen: `SNAP OFF THE TOP.` → `IT'S BACK NEXT WEEK.` → `EASE OUT THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: Kusala is usually translated wholesome, or skillful. In everyday Pali it can describe someone skilled at a craft, or someone well and healthy. Its opposite is akusala: unwholesome, unskillful. Sariputta begins by naming unwholesome actions, ten of them, a list later called the ten unwholesome courses of action: killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, idle chatter, covetousness, ill will and wrong view. Three of the body, four of speech, three of the mind. Then the roots. What is the root of the unwholesome? Greed is a root. Hatred is a root. Delusion is a root. And the wholesome? Abstaining from those ten. And its roots: non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion. Notice the shape. Sariputta doesn't stop at the list of actions. The ten are the weeds above the ground. The roots are what keep them coming back. You can stop lying for a week by force of will, but if the greed or fear underneath is untouched, the lie grows back. Notice too that the wholesome roots are described with a not: non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion. But some teachers explain them positively as well: non-greed shows up as generosity, non-hatred as kindness, non-delusion as wisdom. So a single generous act isn't only a nice thing done. It's a root being watered. And here's why Sariputta starts here, in a talk about right view. Seeing clearly begins with seeing what's actually driving what you do. Not to feel guilty about it. To know which root to tend.
screen: `KUSALA: WHOLESOME, SKILLFUL.` · `TEN UNWHOLESOME ACTIONS.` · `GREED, HATRED, DELUSION.` · `GENEROSITY, KINDNESS, WISDOM.` · then, large: `ROOTS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice one root at work. Sit, and let the last day replay gently. Find one moment you acted, spoke or thought something you're not proud of, a small one. Don't scold yourself. Just look underneath it: was the root wanting, or aversion, or confusion? Then find one moment you acted well, and look under that too: generosity, kindness, or clear seeing? Rest with that root a few breaths. The bell holds the time.
Kusala. Wholesome, skillful: actions rooted in non-greed, non-hatred and non-delusion, the roots Sariputta names first in his talk on right view.
Your line: roots. Today, when you catch yourself about to say or do something you'll regret, ask which root it's growing from. Then water a different one. Day three hundred fifty-five.

match.prompt: match each root to its opposite.

myth: the ten unwholesome actions include actions of the mind
three of body, four of speech, three of mind: covetousness, ill will, wrong view.
Sariputta begins his talk on right view with the twelve links
he begins with wholesome and unwholesome actions and their roots.
kusala can also describe someone skilled at a craft
its everyday sense includes skilled and well.

fork.setup: you've told a small lie to avoid an awkward conversation. by Sariputta's teaching, what's worth looking at?
options: only the lie itself.
the root underneath it: greed, hatred or delusion.
who made the conversation awkward.
fork.reveal: Sariputta names the actions, then the roots they grow from; tending the root is what keeps the weed from coming back.

original.note: Pali kusala: wholesome, skillful; its opposite is akusala, unwholesome.

trapdoor: what you thought: wholesome means being a good person.
what it means: actions are wholesome or unwholesome by their roots: greed, hatred and delusion, or their opposites.
what a scholar hears: MN 9 names lobha, dosa and moha as the akusala-mūla and alobha, adosa and amoha as the kusala-mūla, and lists the ten akusala-kammapatha.

sources.ref: MN 9 (Sammaditthi Sutta), the wholesome and unwholesome and their roots

356.title: Worldly right view
356.hook: that giving bears fruit, that deeds matter, that there are good teachers (MN 117)
356.howItsDone: In Theravada lay practice, right view is often lived as confidence in kamma: giving to monks and the needy, honoring parents and teachers, and trusting that good actions bear good fruit.

segments.voice: Yesterday: kusala, and your line, roots. Did you catch which root a moment was growing from, and water a different one? Day three hundred fifty-six.

Six in the morning, a village road, and a grandmother who has never read a sutta is already waiting with a pot of rice for the monks' bowls. She does this every day. She's honest at the market. She tells her grandchildren that what you do comes back to you, that your parents deserve respect, that there are good people in the world worth listening to. Does she have right view? Or is right view only for scholars who can recite the twelve links? The Buddha's answer, in a sutta about the path's factors, is that there are two kinds of right view. And the grandmother has the first one. Today, worldly right view.
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER WHO NEVER READ A SUTTA.` → `RICE, HONESTY, RESPECT.` → `TWO KINDS OF RIGHT VIEW.`

segments.voice: The sutta is number one hundred seventeen in the Middle-Length Discourses, the Great Forty. In it the Buddha says right view is twofold. There's right view that is still bound up with the world, sharing in merit and ripening in good results. And there's right view that is noble, beyond the world: the wisdom of someone who has entered the path for real. Then he spells out the worldly kind, as a list of things a person holds to be so. There is what is given: giving bears fruit. There is fruit and result of good and bad deeds. There is this world and the other world. There is mother and father, which the commentaries read as: they matter, and are owed gratitude. There are beings reborn spontaneously. And there are good, well-practiced teachers in the world who have seen these things for themselves and make them known. Notice what's on that list. Not complicated philosophy. Basic confidence that actions have consequences, that generosity isn't wasted, that parents and teachers count. In Pali, the action is kamma, karma in Sanskrit, and its result is vipaka, the ripening. The Buddha doesn't call worldly right view second-rate; teachers often describe it as the ground the noble kind grows from. And again and again in the same sutta he says right view comes first, because it lets you tell wrong view as wrong and right view as right. So the grandmother at the roadside with her rice pot isn't doing something less than the scholar. She's standing on the first floor of the same house. Modern Buddhists hold different views about rebirth and other worlds, and teachers address that in different ways. The list's center holds across them: deeds matter.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF RIGHT VIEW.` · `GIVING BEARS FRUIT.` · `KAMMA AND ITS RIPENING.` · `THE GROUND THE NOBLE KIND GROWS FROM.` · then, large: `DEEDS MATTER.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to notice one fruit of a deed. Sit and breathe. Think of one kind thing someone did for you long ago, a teacher who stayed late, a stranger who helped. Notice whether it still lives in you. That's a fruit. Then think of one small thing you did for someone else, and imagine it ripening in them, quietly, somewhere you'll never see. Let both rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Worldly right view. The everyday confidence that giving bears fruit, deeds have results, parents matter and good teachers exist: the ground of the path.
Your line: deeds matter. Today, do one small thing as if it will ripen somewhere: hold a door, send a thank-you, clean up a mess you didn't make. Day three hundred fifty-six.

match.prompt: match each piece of worldly right view.
pairs: the wisdom of one on the path

myth: in MN 117 the Buddha says right view is twofold
worldly right view, sharing in merit, and noble right view, beyond the world.
worldly right view is dismissed as useless
the sutta counts it as right view; teachers describe it as the ground of the noble kind.
worldly right view includes that mother and father matter
it's on the list, along with giving, deeds and good teachers.

fork.setup: a grandmother gives rice to monks every morning, is honest at market, and honors her parents. she's never read a sutta. by MN 117, does she have right view?
options: no, only scholars do.
yes, worldly right view.
only if she can recite the twelve links.
fork.reveal: MN 117 counts confidence that giving bears fruit and deeds matter as right view: the worldly kind, ground of the noble kind.

original.note: Pali kamma, Sanskrit karma: intentional action; its result is called vipāka, ripening.

trapdoor: what you thought: right view is only for advanced meditators.
what it means: there's worldly right view too: confidence that deeds matter, the ground of the deeper kind.

what a scholar hears: MN 117 distinguishes sāsava sammā diṭṭhi, with taints and sharing in merit, from ariya anāsava lokuttara sammā diṭṭhi, noble and supramundane, the wisdom faculty of one on the path.

357.title: Views held lightly
357.hook: the raft: even good teachings are for crossing over, not for holding on to (MN 22)
357.tomorrow: The blind men and the elephant
357.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many settings use the raft simile to remind students that teachings and views are tools for freedom, and some traditions, Zen among them, stress not clinging even to the words of the teaching.

segments.voice: Yesterday: worldly right view, and your line, deeds matter. Did you do one small thing as if it would ripen somewhere? Today closes the week. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

The raft story has come up more than once on this path. But the sutta it comes from has a darker opening. A monk named Arittha, whom the text calls a former vulture trainer, has decided that, as he understands the teaching, the things the Buddha called obstacles aren't really obstacles at all. The other monks can't talk him out of it. So the Buddha calls him in. Before the raft, there's a snake.
screen: `A MONK SURE OF HIS READING.` → `THE OTHERS CAN'T MOVE HIM.` → `BEFORE THE RAFT, A SNAKE.`

segments.voice: The sutta is the Simile of the Water Snake, number twenty-two in the Middle-Length Discourses. The Buddha says some people learn the teaching, but don't look into its meaning with wisdom. They learn it in order to criticize others, or to win debates. They're like a man looking for a water snake who grabs it by the tail. It turns and bites him. A teaching grabbed the wrong way can hurt the one who grabs it. Then the raft. A man comes to a wide river. This side is dangerous; the far side is safe; there's no ferry and no bridge. He gathers grass, sticks and branches, binds them into a raft, and paddles across. On the far bank he thinks: this raft was so useful, I'll lift it onto my head and carry it wherever I go. Would that be the right thing to do with a raft? No, say the monks. He should haul it up onto dry land, or set it adrift in the water, and go on his way. In the same way, the Buddha says, he has taught the Dhamma like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to. And he adds: you should let go even of good teachings, how much more of bad ones. It's said in a sutta that began with a monk gripping his own reading of the teaching. Views aren't useless. They're boats. And looking back over the week: seeing dependent arising as seeing the Dhamma, the four truths closed, eight spokes, right view as a lens, the three roots, worldly right view. Today's lesson holds all of them: carry them lightly.
screen: `ARITTHA'S WRONG GRASP.` · `A SNAKE GRABBED BY THE TAIL.` · `A RAFT ON THE FAR BANK.` · `LET GO EVEN OF GOOD TEACHINGS.` · then, large: `A RAFT, NOT A HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to hold one opinion loosely. Sit and settle. Bring to mind an opinion you hold firmly: about politics, a family matter, the right way to load a dishwasher. Feel how it sits in you, maybe a tightness, a readiness to argue. Now picture it as a raft: useful, built for a purpose. Without throwing it away, imagine setting it down on the bank for a moment. Notice how your hands feel. The bell holds the time.
Views held lightly. The teaching is a raft for crossing, not something to grasp like a snake by the tail, and not a house to live in.
Your line: a raft, not a house. Today, in one disagreement, ask yourself whether you're using your view to cross a river, or carrying it on your head. Day three hundred fifty-seven.

a monk clinging to a wrong view
where the raft is left behind

myth: the raft story says teachings are useless
the raft got the man across; it's useful, just not for carrying on your head.
the same sutta warns against grabbing a teaching like a snake by the tail
learning it to criticize or win debates can bite the one who grabs it.
the Buddha says to let go even of good teachings
how much more, he adds, of bad ones.

fork.setup: you've crossed a dangerous river on a raft you built. you're on the safe bank. what do you do with the raft?
options: carry it on your head wherever you go.
haul it onto dry land, or set it adrift, and go on.
go back and cross again.
fork.reveal: the monks agree he should haul it ashore or set it adrift and go on; the Buddha says the Dhamma is like a raft, for crossing over, not for holding on to.

original.note: Pali kulla: a raft; the sutta speaks of the Dhamma as kullūpama, like a raft.

trapdoor: what you thought: the raft story means Buddhism doesn't take its teachings seriously.
what it means: teachings are serious tools for crossing, and grasping them wrongly can hurt.

what a scholar hears: MN 22 pairs the water-snake simile (alagadda) with the raft (kulla), aimed at Ariṭṭha, said to be a former vulture trainer, and adds dhammā pi vo pahātabbā pageva adhammā: even dhammas are to be let go, how much more non-dhammas.
